svg.title: Three account tiers that share no identifier with each other
svg.desc: Three side-by-side columns representing the everyday, community and exploration account tiers, separated by dashed lines marked as non-overlapping. The everyday tier is the identity you share with work, family and long-term friends, holding email, social media, banking and streaming, on the assumption that family or colleagues seeing it is fine. The community tier is the identity used with LGBTQ+ friends, community events and content about sexual orientation; it shares nothing with the everyday tier, so you can take part in the community without being linked back, and its profile picture uses no photo that appears anywhere family or colleagues can see. The exploration tier covers dating apps, anonymous communities and test accounts, the highest-risk and shortest-lived of the three. The bar at the top states the basis of the separation: no shared email, no shared username, no shared browser, no shared password manager folder. The bar at the bottom lists what each tier needs of its own: an email address, a browser profile, a password manager vault and a two-factor group.
svg.text: no email, no username, no browser
Long-lived, tied to your legal name
Family or colleagues seeing this is fine.
You can take part without being linked back
to the everyday tier. The profile picture
uses no photo family or colleagues can see.
The highest-risk tier. Keep it separate from
the community tier as well, since location and
photos expose more here than anywhere else.
Four things each tier needs of its own
Its own email address (aliases can grow
several public addresses out of one mailbox),
its own browser profile, its own password
manager vault, its own two-factor group.
At sign-up, avoid the reverse matching
platforms run on phone numbers and contact
lists. Once an account exists, watch for
reverse image search on the avatar, reused
usernames, posting times and writing style.
